Words, in plain language

Every word the book teaches, in the order of the alphabet, with the chapter that first explains it. 236 words.

ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVW

A

A/B test
showing a change to a random half of users and comparing them with the other half; the randomising is what lets you say the change caused the difference Chapter 44
AARRR
five stages of growth, each given one countable event: acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue Chapter 43
abstention
a system deciding not to answer, and saying so, when it does not have the evidence; it is a product behaviour to be designed, not a sentence in an instruction Chapter 35
acceptance criteria
the conditions a piece of work must meet to count as done, each written so it can be tested Chapter 7
access control
rules that decide which user may see which document or chunk, enforced in the application and data layer, not asked of the model Chapter 35
activation moment
the first time a user gets the value the product promises; everything before it is cost to the user Chapter 43
agentic search
letting a model run several searches itself, read what comes back and rewrite its query, using a loop Chapter 23
AI agent
a model, a set of functions it may ask for, a loop, and a rule for when to stop Chapter 20
AI value chain
the layers an AI product is built on: infrastructure, models, tooling and, on top, the applications that people use; each layer gets its advantage from something different Chapter 31
allowlist
a list of the only things a system is permitted to do; anything not on it is refused Chapter 45
answer key
the test set for the guard: for every example sentence, exactly what should be found and what should happen to it, kept in numbered versions Chapter 12
API
a way for one program to ask another for something in a fixed format, like an order slip handed across a counter Chapter 9
API key
a long secret code that tells a provider who is asking, and whom to bill; anyone who has it can spend your money Chapter 9
architecture decision record
a short note recording a significant technical decision: the alternatives, the choice, the evidence, the consequences, and what would make you revisit it Chapter 40
attack surface
all the places where an outsider can feed something into a system or reach something it can do; every tool, input and connection adds to it Chapter 39
attention
the part of a transformer that works out, for each token, which other tokens matter most for predicting what comes next Chapter 8
audit trail
a record, kept separately from the work itself, of who did what, when, under which rule and with what result, enough for someone to reconstruct an incident Chapter 39

B

B2B
business to business: a product sold to companies, where the person who pays is often not the person who uses it Chapter 2
B2C
business to consumer: a product sold to individual people, who are both the buyers and the users Chapter 2
bottom-up estimate
a size estimate built from customers you can count, multiplied by what each would pay, instead of a slice taken from an industry report Chapter 4
bounded agent
an AI agent given hard limits on steps, time and cost, a state it keeps explicitly, and a "cannot resolve" ending, so that it always stops Chapter 36

C

caching
letting the provider remember the processed start of a request so that, if it is identical next time, the later request is cheaper and faster Chapter 21
canary release
showing a change first to a small share of users, with the old version ready, before everyone gets it Chapter 38
cascade
a design that sends every request to the cheapest thing that might work and passes on only what fails a check to the next, dearer one Chapter 26
case study
a one- or two-page account of a project: the problem and its evidence, your decisions and the options you rejected, the trade-offs, the results with numbers, what failed, and what you would do next Chapter 47
changelog
the short public list of what changed in each release, written for users in practical terms Chapter 46
chunk
one piece of a longer document, small enough to be stored and sent on its own Chapter 14
chunking
splitting long documents into chunks, which means deciding where to cut Chapter 14
claim audit
taking ten claims from an AI-written summary and checking each against its source, marking each supported, partly supported or unsupported Chapter 45
classifier
a program that puts each input into one of a fixed set of categories, such as PAN, Aadhaar, mobile number or none of these Chapter 13
code check
a few lines of ordinary code that test one thing about an answer automatically, such as whether a quoted phrase is really in the message; free to run on every change Chapter 25
cohort
a group of users who started in the same period, followed together over time Chapter 44
compaction
shrinking a long conversation by summarising its middle and keeping the beginning and the end Chapter 21
competitor teardown
a side-by-side look at each alternative: who it is for, what it costs, where it is strong and where customers complain Chapter 4
context engineering
deciding what goes into each request, in what order and what is left out: the instructions, examples, evidence, history and tool results Chapter 21
context judge
the third part of the guard: it reads the few sentences the first two parts could not settle and decides whether they point to a person Chapter 7
context window
the limit on how much text a model can take in at once, counting both what you send and what it writes back Chapter 8
contextual retrieval
before storing each chunk, adding a sentence that says where it sits in its document, so that an orphaned chunk keeps its meaning Chapter 23
contribution margin
what a customer leaves you after the costs that grow with them, as a share of what they pay Chapter 42
conversation history
the earlier messages of a chat, which an app has to send again with each new message if it wants the model to seem to remember Chapter 10
cost of delay
what you lose for every week an option waits Chapter 5

D

dark pattern
a design that tricks users into acting against their own interest, such as a pre-ticked box, false scarcity or a hidden cancellation Chapter 43
data contract
the unspoken assumptions one part of a system makes about the data it receives, such as that a field will be present and a list will not be empty Chapter 33
data residency
the country or region where a provider stores and processes what you send it Chapter 28
decision log
a running page where you write down each important decision, the evidence behind it, and what would make you change your mind Chapter 1
decision memo
a short document written so a busy person can decide after reading its first paragraph Chapter 6
deletion drill
pretending a customer has asked for their data to be deleted and finding every place it lives, to learn which ones you cannot reach Chapter 29
delivery
the part of making a product where you build it well: the plan, the specification, the code, the quality Chapter 2
dependency
anything you need from outside your own team in order to finish: another team's work, a supplier, access to data, an approval Chapter 6
design partner
an early user who agrees to use an unfinished product and tell you honestly what they find, in return for something fair Chapter 46
diagnosis
the first part of a strategy: an honest account of what the real challenge is, before saying what to do about it Chapter 5
discovery
the part of making a product where you find out whether a problem is real and worth solving Chapter 2
distribution
the part of making a product where people find it, try it and keep using it Chapter 2
document audit
counting, from a random sample, how much of a collection is clean digital text, how much is scanned, and how much has its meaning in tables and layout, before anything is built Chapter 27
DPDP Act
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which sets duties for organisations that handle personal data, far beyond finding and hiding it Chapter 29

E

edge case
an unusual input or situation that breaks things the ordinary cases never touch Chapter 7
embedding
a long list of numbers that places a piece of text on a map of meanings, so that texts meaning similar things get similar numbers even when they share no words Chapter 16
environment variable
a value kept outside the code, in the place a program runs, which is where passwords and API keys belong Chapter 33
error analysis
reading a hundred real outputs, writing down in your own words what went wrong in each, grouping the notes, naming the groups and counting them Chapter 25
event taxonomy
the list of events a product records, with a naming rule everyone follows, such as object_action in lower case and past tense Chapter 44
evidence pack
the set of artifacts that lets somebody else check your claims instead of trusting them Chapter 41
exit cost
what it would cost, in money, time and risk, to leave a provider and move to another; a vendor can win on quality and still lock you in for years Chapter 40
experiment runner
a reusable program that records, for every experiment, the inputs, outputs, settings, timings and errors, so a result can be reproduced and compared Chapter 33

F

failure class
a kind of failure and not a single instance of one; it is what makes ten tests meaningful instead of ten anecdotes Chapter 41
failure threshold
the result, written down before a pilot starts, below which you will call it a failure Chapter 32
feasibility
whether the team can actually build it with the time, skills, data and money it has Chapter 2
feature flag
a switch in the running system that turns a change on for some users and off for others, without a new release Chapter 45
findings document
a rough, factual record of what broke, the evidence, the root cause, the fix, and what was deliberately left unsolved; the opposite of a brochure Chapter 41
fine-tuning
training a model further on examples of your own, so that it behaves in a consistent way; it teaches behaviour, not facts Chapter 31
five whys
asking "why?" again and again about each answer, to get from a symptom towards its causes Chapter 3
fixed workflow
a sequence of steps decided in advance and written into code, with a model used only for the steps that need judgement Chapter 36
flywheel
a loop in which using the product makes it better, which brings more use; the workflow kind is usually the strongest Chapter 42
Fogg behaviour model
the idea that a behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt meet at the same moment; if it is not happening, check them in reverse order Chapter 43

G

generative AI
AI that produces new content, such as text, images or code, instead of only giving a label or a number Chapter 8
Git
a tool that saves every version of your work, so you can see what changed and go back to any earlier version Chapter 33
golden dataset
the versioned, representative set of cases, with expected behaviour, that defines what good means for a system; it needs a version number so a result can be rerun Chapter 38
graceful degradation
when part of a system fails, continuing to work in a reduced but safe way, instead of failing altogether Chapter 40
gross margin
revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product; for AI products much of that cost is a model or hosting bill Chapter 42
grounded answer
an answer written from evidence the system supplied, and traceable to it, instead of from what the model happens to remember Chapter 18
growth loop
a cycle in which one user's actions bring in the next user, so that the output feeds back into the input Chapter 43
guardrail metric
a number that must not get worse while you chase the key results Chapter 6
guiding policy
the second part of a strategy: the overall approach you will take to the challenge, including what you will refuse to do Chapter 5

H

hallucination
a confident, well-formed answer that is invented; it happens because the model predicts likely text, and "I do not know" is rarely the likeliest text Chapter 11
harness
everything around the model that makes it a product: the code that builds its context, runs its tools, keeps state, enforces rules, checks quality and records what happened Chapter 45
HTTP
the set of rules programs use to send requests and replies across the internet, with a number on each reply that says whether it worked Chapter 33
human oversight
a person who can see the evidence for an output, and can reject it; watching outputs go by does not count Chapter 29
hybrid pricing
a platform fee that includes some usage, then a charge for what goes beyond it; predictable for the buyer and protective of your margin Chapter 42
hybrid search
running keyword search and meaning-based search together and combining the two rankings, so you do not have to choose between them Chapter 23

I

idempotency
the property of an action that can safely be run twice, or is protected so that running it twice has only one effect; it decides whether a retry is safe Chapter 36
incident review
a short written account, made after something goes wrong, of what happened, why, and which check would have caught it Chapter 45
inference
using a finished model to answer a request; it costs money each time and does not change the model Chapter 8
informed consent
a person's agreement, given after being told plainly what is collected, where it goes, what could go wrong and how to withdraw Chapter 46
ingestion
the step of reading documents into a system, including scanning, parsing and splitting them; whatever is lost here is lost for good Chapter 35
input metric
a number the team can change directly that you expect to move the outcome Chapter 6
instruction tuning
the second stage of making a model, in which it is trained on examples of instructions paired with good answers so that it follows instructions Chapter 8

J

job to be done
the progress a person is trying to make in their life, which they "hire" a product to help with Chapter 3
JSON
a plain way of writing information as labels and values inside curly braces, which nearly every API uses Chapter 9

K

key result
one of the three or four numbers under an objective that show whether you got there; it measures what changed for people, not what you shipped Chapter 6
keyword search
finding text by matching the words of the question against the words in the documents; it compares spelling, not meaning Chapter 15
kill criterion
a condition, written down in advance, that means you stop the work Chapter 6
kill switch
a flag that sends traffic to a simple non-AI path immediately, with no new deployment; it only works if that path exists and has been tested recently Chapter 30

L

language model
a program that has learned, from a vast amount of writing, to predict what text comes next; it is what sits behind a chatbot Chapter 8
latency
the time between asking and getting an answer, which users feel as speed Chapter 22
latency budget
the total time a request may take, divided among the stages it passes through, so that the slowest stage is found and owned Chapter 40
leaderboard
a published ranking of models by their scores on someone else's tests Chapter 34
leading question
a question that suggests the answer the asker is hoping for Chapter 3
least privilege
giving a system only the access it actually needs, so that if it is fooled the damage is limited Chapter 39
lethal trifecta
the three things that together make a system dangerous: access to private data, exposure to text that outsiders can write, and a way to send something out Chapter 24
LLM judge
a model that grades another model's output; cheap and fast, but it has biases and must be checked against your own grading before it is trusted Chapter 25
lock-in
being tied to one provider because leaving would cost too much, in rewriting, remeasuring or lost features Chapter 31

M

mask
to hide part of a detail but keep its shape, for example 98******12 Chapter 7
MCP
Model Context Protocol: a standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data, so that any compliant tool fits any compliant application, like a plug and a socket Chapter 36
metadata filtering
removing, before any scoring, the chunks that cannot be right, using labels attached to them such as version, dates and who may see them Chapter 23
minimum detectable effect
the smallest change worth detecting; it sets how many users a test needs Chapter 44
model selection card
a short, versioned page recording the task, the quality target, the limits on data, speed and cost, the options tried, the evidence and the fallback, so that a reviewer can see exactly why a model was chosen Chapter 34
MoSCoW
a way of agreeing scope by sorting items into Must, Should, Could and Won't Chapter 5
multimodal
able to take in more than text, such as pages, pictures, tables and speech, which changes what counts as evidence and how it is traced Chapter 37
must-keep list
for each document, the facts a reader must not lose, against which every summary is checked Chapter 13
MVP
minimum viable product: the smallest thing that tests your riskiest assumption with real users Chapter 7

N

name-and-place finder
the second part of the guard: it finds details with no fixed shape, such as a person's name, an address or an employer Chapter 7
network effect
the product getting better for everyone as more people use it, which is not the same as users bringing in other users Chapter 43
North Star
one sentence saying what value your customers get, and one number that measures it Chapter 5

O

observability
being able to see, from the records a system keeps, what it did and why, without guessing Chapter 38
observation session
a meeting in which you give someone a real task and watch them do it without helping, noting the same things each time Chapter 46
OCR
optical character recognition: software that turns a picture of text into text, usually with a few mistakes Chapter 27
OKR
objectives and key results: a goal written in words, with a few numbers that show you reached it Chapter 6
open-weight model
a model whose weights are published, so you can download it and run it on your own computers instead of calling someone else's Chapter 31
opportunity tree
a drawing that starts from the outcome you want, branches into the needs people described in interviews, and ends in possible solutions Chapter 4
orphaned chunk
a chunk that makes no sense once cut out of its document, because it refers to something that was in the piece before Chapter 14
outcome pricing
charging for each successful result, so that price follows value; it needs an agreed, measurable definition of success Chapter 42

P

p95
the time that 95 out of 100 requests beat; it shows the slow tail that an average hides Chapter 38
parser
the program that turns a file such as a PDF into text and structure; its mistakes are invisible to everything that comes after it Chapter 35
pattern checker
the first part of the guard: it finds details that always have the same shape, such as a PAN or a mobile number, using fixed rules Chapter 7
persona
a short description of one type of user, built only from what interviews showed Chapter 3
PII
personally identifiable information: any detail that can point to one real person, such as a name, a phone number or an identity number Chapter 1
pilot
a limited trial designed to show whether a feature helps the business, which states in advance what result would count as failure Chapter 32
pinned version
a model version that you have fixed by name, so that the provider cannot change it underneath you without telling you Chapter 30
positioning statement
one sentence saying who a product is for and why it is different from the alternatives Chapter 4
PRD
product requirements document: the paper that says what to build and why, starting from the problem and its evidence Chapter 7
pre-mortem
a meeting where everyone imagines the project has failed and writes down why, before it starts Chapter 6
pre-training
the first and most expensive stage of making a model, in which it learns to predict the next token over a vast amount of text Chapter 8
precision
of everything the tool flagged, the share that really was what it claimed; if it flagged 100 and 80 were real, precision is 80 percent Chapter 17
predictive AI
AI that gives a label or a number for one specific task, such as whether a message is spam Chapter 8
problem statement
one or two sentences saying who has the problem, what it is, and what it costs them today Chapter 3
product risk
one of the four things that can sink a product: nobody wants it, nobody can use it, it cannot be built, or it cannot pay for itself Chapter 2
product sense
the ability to choose a user, find their real problem and propose a sensible solution, which interviewers test with questions such as "design a product for busy parents" Chapter 47
product-led growth
winning customers by letting users sign up and get value on their own, with some of them upgrading; it fits when value shows in minutes and the price is low Chapter 43
production delta
the list of everything missing between a working prototype and a running service, such as identity, retries, queues, monitoring, secrets, backups and rollback Chapter 40
project memory
a plain file kept with the code, holding the rules and habits of the project, loaded at the start of every run of a coding assistant Chapter 45
prompt
the text you send a model, which can include instructions, examples and the material you want it to work on Chapter 11
prompt injection
text inside material a system is asked to read that gives the model instructions, which the model may follow because it cannot reliably tell your instructions from words it was asked to read Chapter 24
prototype
a rough, cheap version made to learn something before the real one exists Chapter 7
provenance
the record of where something came from, so that a claim or a decision can be traced to its source, version and the code that produced it Chapter 34
Python
the programming language most AI work is written in; for a product manager, a way of saying exactly what an experiment does Chapter 33

Q

quasi-identifier
a detail that is harmless alone but can point to one person when combined with others, such as age, village and a rare illness Chapter 7

R

reasoning model
a model that writes out its working, trying an approach and checking it, before it gives the answer; you pay for that working on every request, in money and in waiting time Chapter 22
recall
of all the real items there were to find, the share the tool found; if there were 100 and it found 90, recall is 90 percent Chapter 17
red team
people whose job is to attack a system on purpose, so its weaknesses are found by them first Chapter 39
redact
to remove a detail completely, for example by replacing it with the word [PAN] Chapter 7
refusal
a system saying plainly that it cannot do something and offering a route to a person, which is designed on purpose and not left as an accident Chapter 32
regression
a change that makes a system worse at something it used to do well Chapter 38
release gate
an automatic check that runs the golden dataset against a change and blocks the release if any number falls below its threshold Chapter 38
repository
the folder, kept in Git, that holds all of a project's work and its history Chapter 33
reranking
fetching many candidate pieces cheaply, then having a slower, more careful model read the question and each piece together and put the best few on top Chapter 23
residual risk
the risk that remains after the controls are in place, which should be written down and not assumed away Chapter 39
retention
how long a provider keeps what you send it, which may be longer than the time it takes to answer Chapter 28
retrieval
the step of finding the pieces of your documents that look relevant to a question Chapter 18
retrieval-augmented generation
RAG: a design in which a system first finds the pieces of your documents that look relevant to a question, then gives them to a model along with the question so it writes its answer from them Chapter 18
RICE
a way of scoring options by Reach times Impact times Confidence, divided by Effort Chapter 5
risk register
a table listing each risk with its owner, its control, the evidence the control works, and what risk remains Chapter 39
risk tier
a level, set by how much harm a wrong answer could do, that decides how much documentation, checking and evidence a system needs; the use sets the tier, not the technology Chapter 29
riskiest assumption
the thing that must be true for your idea to work and that you are least sure of, so the one to test first Chapter 3
roadmap
a plan that shows what a team will work on and roughly when; the useful kind promises outcomes in three columns, Now, Next and Later, instead of dates Chapter 6
role matrix
a table with the skills that real job advertisements ask for down one side and the roles across the top, in which you mark each skill as proven, partly proven or missing for yourself Chapter 47
rollback
returning to the previous version of the code, which needs a new deployment and does not help when both versions share the same bad behaviour Chapter 30
rollback trigger
a measurable condition, written down beforehand, that obliges someone to undo a release Chapter 45
routing
sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, and only the hard ones to a stronger and dearer one Chapter 34
rule-keeper
the fourth part of the guard: it decides what to do with each detail found, such as remove it, mask it, let it through or ask Chapter 7

S

SAM
serviceable addressable market: the part of the TAM you could actually serve with what you have Chapter 4
schema
a formal description of exactly what shape an answer must have, which the provider enforces while the model is writing Chapter 19
scoreboard
the table that counts, for each version of the tool, what it found, what it missed and what it wrongly flagged Chapter 12
SDK
software development kit: a small library plus a demo that another developer can add to their own product without building the feature themselves Chapter 41
seat pricing
charging for each user of the product, per month; easy for a buyer to budget but unfair when heavy users cost far more to serve than light ones Chapter 42
shadow AI
staff using consumer AI tools on their own, often by pasting in internal documents, because the tools are useful and nothing sanctioned is as good Chapter 29
similarity score
a number from about 0 to 1 saying how close two embeddings are; it means little until you know what clearly good and clearly bad matches score Chapter 16
SOM
serviceable obtainable market: the part of the SAM you could realistically win in about three years Chapter 4
speaker attribution
working out who said which words in a recording; it looks technical and behaves like a privacy decision Chapter 37
speech-to-text
software that turns recorded speech into written words; it is the first stage of any voice system and the first place meaning can be lost Chapter 37
sprint
a fixed period, usually one or two weeks, that a team plans, builds, shows and reviews Chapter 7
staging
a copy of the live system where changes are tried first, so that a bad one never reaches real users Chapter 40
stakeholder
anyone who can help or stop a project, or who is affected by it Chapter 6
STAR method
a way to tell a story about your own past in four parts: situation, task, action and result, with most of the time spent on what you did Chapter 47
state machine
a workflow in which your code fixes every step and every allowed move from one step to the next Chapter 45
stateless
keeping nothing between requests: every call starts from nothing, and the model does not know you spoke a moment ago Chapter 10
status code
the number on an HTTP reply: 200 means it worked, a 4xx number means the request was wrong, and a 5xx number means the server failed Chapter 33
status quo
what people do today, including doing nothing; usually the strongest competitor Chapter 4
step limit
the maximum number of rounds an AI agent may take before it must stop, set by the program and not left to the model Chapter 20
streaming
sending an answer to the screen piece by piece as it is written, instead of waiting until it is complete Chapter 22
structured output
an answer in named, typed fields that a program can read, instead of a paragraph that a person reads Chapter 19
sub-agent
a helper given one part of a large task, which works in its own separate context so that the main one stays small Chapter 45
support log
a running record of every request for help, with its category and the account it came from, read weekly as evidence about the product Chapter 46
system card
a one-page description of an AI system: what it is for, what data it uses, how it was tested, what it gets wrong and what it must not be used for Chapter 29
system prompt
the standing instructions an app sends with every request, saying who the assistant is and what it must and must not do Chapter 11
system-design interview
a conversation in which you are asked to design an AI feature aloud, and judged on your reasoning about approach, evaluation, failure, cost and rollout, not on code Chapter 47

T

take-home
a piece of work set by an employer to be done alone within a time limit, which tests how you work when no one is watching Chapter 47
TAM
total addressable market: everyone who has the problem, at the price you would charge Chapter 4
task type
which of five kinds of job a request really is: classify, extract, summarise, rewrite or generate Chapter 12
temperature
a setting that decides how often a model picks a less likely next token; low gives similar answers each time, high gives more variety Chapter 11
test set
a collection of real or realistic examples, each with the correct answer written down beforehand, used to measure a system Chapter 12
time-box
a fixed amount of time given to uncertain work, with a decision at the end of it Chapter 7
time-to-value
how long a new user takes to reach the activation moment, measured from sign-up Chapter 43
token
a piece of text, often a whole word and sometimes part of one, which is the unit that models read and that providers charge by Chapter 8
token budget
a plan that gives each part of a request its share of tokens, with someone who owns the total and knows what to cut first Chapter 21
tool calling
letting a model ask your program to run a function, by naming the function and its arguments; the program runs it and sends the result back Chapter 20
tool contract
the precise written agreement for one function a model may call: its name, what it does and does not do, its parameters, its errors, its side effects and who is allowed to call it Chapter 36
tool description
the few lines of text that tell a model what a function does, what it returns and what it does not; the model chooses a function by reading them, so a vague one is a bug Chapter 20
toolchain
the set of tools a team uses to build and run a product, thought of as slots to be filled, each with a job to do Chapter 45
trace record
the saved record of one request's whole path through the system: input, versions, steps, timings, cost and outcome Chapter 38
tracking plan
the shared document that lists every event, its properties, when it fires and who owns it, which engineers build from and analysts trust Chapter 44
transformer
the design that almost all modern language models are built on, whose key part is attention Chapter 8

U

usability
whether people can work out how to use something without help Chapter 2
usability test
watching a real person try to complete a task with a prototype, without helping them Chapter 7
usage block
the part of every reply that says how many tokens went in and how many came out, which is what you are charged for Chapter 9
usage pricing
charging for each unit used, such as each message or call, so that revenue follows cost; buyers cannot predict the bill and may ration use Chapter 42
user interview
a conversation held to learn what a person actually did and needed, not whether they would like your idea Chapter 3
user story
one piece of value described from the user's side: who they are, what they want, and why Chapter 7

V

validation
checking an answer against rules after it arrives, for example whether a required field is present or a quoted phrase really appears in the message Chapter 19
value proposition
a plain statement of who you serve, what job you do for them and why you are better than the alternatives Chapter 5
verifier
a check, such as a test, that tells an agent whether its own change worked, without a person reading every line Chapter 45
vertical slice
